claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains spatially distinct phases.
The distinct eutectic phases have different oxidation or electrochemical potentials.
Differential oxidation of the phases creates localized galvanic cells.
Mechanical wear continuously exposes fresh alloy material.
Micro-galvanic interactions combined with repeated exposure of fresh material synergistically accelerate corrosion.
Micro-galvanic interactions combined with repeated exposure of fresh material synergistically accelerate wear.
Phase boundaries promote galvanic coupling because the eutectic phases have different oxidation kinetics.
Localized micro-galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries preferentially degrades the more anodic phase.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics.
Wear removes protective oxide scales and repeatedly re-exposes fresh material.
The repeated oxide-removal and micro-galvanic-corrosion cycle raises total degradation beyond the sum of separate wear and corrosion effects.
Combined wear and corrosion will produce significantly greater total degradation than the matched separate-exposure baselines.
Under combined exposure, the more anodic phase will exhibit an enhanced corrosion rate.
Under combined exposure, wear volume will increase because oxide layers are removed and micro-galvanic interfaces are repeatedly exposed.
The mechanism requires a temperature high enough to produce significant oxidation kinetics.
The mechanism requires wear sufficient to remove protective oxide layers.
The mechanism requires sufficiently different electrochemical potentials between the phases.
The proposed boundary conditions exclude wear severe enough to cause complete amorphization of the microstructure.
Homogenizing the microstructure by heat treatment is expected to reduce phase-related galvanic coupling.
Similar or greater coupled degradation in homogenized samples, or failure to detect localized micro-galvanic activity in segregated samples, would falsify the proposed driving mechanism.
